Derogatory Article in "The Economist" about India and 
Indian Bureaucracy  
SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I am raising an iss ue on which large sections of our 
patriotic people are agitated and anguished. The issue is a write-up in The Economist published 
from London. The 8th March, 2008 issue carries an a rticle 'Briefing India's Civil Service', 
'Battling the babu raj'. I have gone through the en tire piece. Sir, it is a worldwide sinister 
propaganda to malign and undermine India and its capabilities. It is really a sinister worldwide 
propaganda to malign and undermine India's Executive. 1 shall read certain extracts for the 
consideration of the House.  
The article says, "Some economists see India's malfunctioning public sector as its biggest 
obstacle to growth". In fact, India is emerging as an economic power in the world and India 
has got a significant growth rate, but this is beca use of the collective efforts made by our 
people. But this write up says that the malfunctioning public sector is the biggest obstacle to 
its growth. Then, it goes on to say, "Part of the problem, such critics say, is that the quality of 
IAS recruits is falling. They identify a number of reasons for this: falling education standards, 
growing competition for talent from the private sector, increasing political interference, and, 
above all"—I would like the House to take note of t his—"caste-based reservations, which 
now retain half of all IAS posts for outcaste and l ow-caste Hindus and members of tribal 
communities". This is how the article has been written, Sir. It is a kind of malice against the 
IAS officers who hail from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. It is a different fact that 
these officers do not find adequate representation in the decision-making of the Government. 
But, having said this, I must say, it is a malice against our Executive and it is a world-wide 
propaganda. The article says, 'Some economists say" , 'some critics'. Who are those 'some 
economists'? Who are those 'some critics'? It is not journalistic ethics and a journal like The 
Economist should not publish such articles about a country like ours.  
India is the largest democracy in the world. We have a vibrant democracy. We have an 
Executive that is answerable to the people and I co ndemn this...

Problems of Indian Workers in us  
SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA (Maharashtra): Sir, I am raising a very important issue about 
the problems being faced by Indian workers in Ameri ca. Hundreds of Indians working in 
shipyards in Mississipi and Texas have been subjected to torture and human trafficking by 
US and Indian recruiting agencies and employers. These workers are reported to have paid 
huge sums of money to recruiters on false promises that they would be given work-based 
permanent residency in America. Instead, they have been given short-term guest workers' 
visa and are made to work in unsatisfactory and exp loitative conditions. It is also alleged 
that the Indian Embassy in America has not taken se rious note of the issue even though 
repeated complaints have been made. Therefore, these workers are reported to have begun a 
Satyagraha and they are moving on foot from New Orleans to Washington D.C. to confront 
the Ambassador for not considering the case seriously. What are the steps being taken by the 
Government to resolve this issue? What are the proposed measures to fight such cases in the 
future?  
Sir, this is a-very serious issue. Most of these Indian workers with false promises by the 
recruiting agencies are being deceived and cheated and all these agencies are minting money. 
Our Ambassador to Washington is not taking any notice of it. He is not trying to help them. 
So, the Foreign Affairs Minister must be asked to look into it personally so that these Indian 
workers could be helped. This is our demand.

196   Special  [RAJYASABHA]  Mentions  
Concern over Rampant Corruption in Public Distribution System  
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): In September, 2007, the Chief Justice of 
India stated that the aam admi has been hit hard by the "deep-rooted corruption" and the 
Public Distribution System (PDS) was in shambles due to this malaise. He mentioned that 
in some States not a single grain reaches the targeted population, adding that corruption 
and police inaction was forcing people to take the law into their own hands. This 
observation has now proved to be prophetic. In Murs hidabad, West Bengal, angry 
villagers pulled out a ration-shop dealer on 7.10.2007 and tied him and his family to a 
free, accusing him of selling subsidised foodgrains meant for them in the open market. 
In another incident in the same area, villagers sought accounts from a dealer and then 
proceeded to ransack the shop. Similar incidents were reported in two other districts as 
well. It's not that West Bengal alone is sitting on a powder keg. A report of the Ministry 
of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution states that in the last three years, Rs. 
31,585.98 crores worth of wheat and rice meant for the poorest of the poor was siphoned 
off from the PDS.  
It is obvious that the Government have failed to deliver food to the poor despite its huge 
network of about 4.5 lakh fair-price shops and a well-laid out supply chain. It is high time 
that some radical reforms were undertaken by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and 
Public Distribution.

Demand for Central Grants for Development of Projects in Karnataka under 
Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission  
SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Sir, it is on rec ord that the Government has 
renewed its commitment on the Jawaharlal Nehru Nati onal Urban Renewal Mission by 
enhancing the budgetary allocation for 2008-09.  
I hope the enhanced outlay for JNNURM for the curre nt year would accommodate the 
long pending proposals from the Government of Karna taka involving 15 projects which 
include improvement works relating to 63 identified  arterial roads, basic services for the 
poor living in slums and works relating to improvem ent of urban infrastructure in Mysore. 
The State level Empowered Committee on Urban Develo pment had cleared these projects.. 
during 2007 for further evaluation and approval by the Government of India in the Ministrs 
of Urban Development.  
Considering the financial constraints still being f aced by the Urban Local Bodies in 
generating resources for basic developmental works, I urge the Centre to expedite evaluation 
and approval of these 15 projects for which detailed project reports have been furnished for 
implementation under the current budget allocation.

PRIVATE MEMBER'S RESOLUTION Menace of 
Increasing Naxal Attacks and Remedial Measures to Combat Attacks  
MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Shri B.S. Gnanadesikan to move the Resolution No. 1.  
SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Deputy Cha irman, sir, with your 
permission, I would like to move the Private Members' Resolution to the following effect:—  
"Having regard to the fact that—  
recently naxal attacks have increased which indicates that the naxalites are consolidating 
their presence across the country;  
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA) in the Chair.]  
state police forces are ill-equipped to counter the naxal attacks and their activities;  
nearly seven hundred people including about two hundred and fifty security personnel 
have been killed in naxal related violence during the last two years;  
absence of awareness against the dangerous prevalence of naxalites in rural and jungle 
villages has caused expansion of naxal network; and 
many security personnel have been killed in naxal prone areas by contracting water-
borne diseases by drinking contaminated water.  
With this background, this House urges upon the Government to look into the problem of 
naxal attacks and increasing naxal activities in al l States and may take war-time steps to 
eliminate and eradicate naxal operations by taking the following measures:  
creation of specialised force to operate along with State police in naxal infected areas;  
the CRPF is to be used as counter-terrorism force in areas where they are deployed together 
with Centralised Special Intelligence Cell for naxal activities;  
provide additional allowance to the jawans posted in naxalite areas in addition to nutritious 
diet allowance;  

Private Member's  [20 MARCH 2008]  Resolution 199  
provide medical facilities to security personnel who are posted in remote naxal infected 
areas;  
accelerate development activities in naxal infected areas;  
involve the local leaders to prevent the people from joining the naxal movement;  
take necessary steps to rehabilitate the naxal cadre who leave the organisation and join 
the mainstream;  
create a central agency to monitor, prevent and era dicate the naxal activities from the 
country so that instead of State-specific, decisions can be made and implemented at 
the Central level."  
Sir, there are four components in my Resolution. The first component is the strengthening 
of police forces in the naxal-affected States. The second component is that the police personnel, 
who are involved in facing the naxal violence,-must  be taken care of and all necessary 
facilities, including, medical facilities, necessary increase of salary, and other allowances, 
must be given to them. The third component is that the people who are affected by the naxal 
violence and the cadres, who want to joint the mainstream from the naxal movement, must 
be taken care of and they must be rehabilitated. Fi nally, fourth component, which I think, 
may raise some eyebrows, and some may agree and some may not agree to it, is that in the 
scenario of regionalism giving way to nationalism and everybody talking about federalism, 
there are several parties which say that a State-specific policy must be there. In the interest 
of national unity and integrity, I want to give a suggestion and I want to start a debate in this 
House today that wherever naxal-affected district — I am not naming the States — could not 
be properly administered by the State administration, wherever cross of funds which flowed 
from the Centre could not be utilised properly, whe rever the funds, allotted to the States 
under various heads and various schemes failed to reach the beneficiaries, in those cases, I 
request the Government to amend the constitutional provisions. There are two provisions in 
the Constitution. One is article 352 which talks ab out proclamation of emergency. That is 
not only external aggression but also armed rebellion. The word 'emergency' is not liked by 
anyone, because once emergency is declared, then su spension of Fundamental Rights and 
other things follow. But, article 355 says, "Duty of the Union to protect States against external 
aggression and internal disturbance". The word used in the Constitution is 'internal disturbance' 
and not 'armed rebellion'. Further, it says, "It will be the duty of the Union to protect every 
State against external aggression and internal disturbance to ensure that the Government of 
every State is carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution." If possible, 
an amendment can be brought in article 355 of the C onstitution that wherever the district 
administration could not properly use the funds mea nt for people, particularly for tribal, 
poor, SC and ST people due to various reasons — I am not saying because of bad governance 
— and could not implement the programmes, the Centr al Government can take action. The 
Government can, at least, consider debate whether s uitable amendment can be brought 
providing for the direct intervention of the Centre  to administer these districts is possible 
where internal disturbance occurs. That is the four th component of my Resolution. I want 
the hon. Members to consider it. In the present pol itical scenario and structure, of course, 
with the consultation of all other allies and partn ers and also with the concurrence and 
consultation of Left parties which are supporting this Government and also in consultation 
with our respectable Opposition parties, for the national interest, I am placing this suggestion 
before the House. There are certain backgrounds for urgency in moving this Resolution. Om  

200   Private Member's  [RAJYASABHA]  Resolution  
hon. Prime Minister has said that this threat will cause internal disturbances and it is very 
serious one. Unless it is checked at proper moment, it will go beyond our control. So, before it 
goes beyond our control, it is time to act. I will justify my reasoning, my argument by giving 
certain figures as to how the Central Government he lped to modernise the police forces, how 
crores of rupees given for naxal-affected States we re not utilised properly. That is the reason 
for proper rehabilitation and other things not bein g done. Sir, that is why, from only a small 
area of naxalite-operations, now, it has spread to Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Bihar, Orissa, 
Maharashtra, Andhra and also parts of Kerala and Ka rnataka. (Interruptions) Sir, in Tamil 
Nadu, there is no naxalite activity. Though my frie nd, Mr. Malaisamy referred naxalite  
activities in Tamil Nadu but because of the proper management, because of the efficient 
police force and because of the efficient bureaucracy, to which Mr. Malaisamy once belonged, I 
think, that has been controlled in the State.  
We had a small problem in the Dharmapuri District b ut that was solved because of 
efficiency of administration. Recently also, we identified some people in Theni District but 
because of the prompt action taken by the state Gov ernment and the police force, their 
attempts have been foiled. That is important. Sir, I am saying all this because some States act 
quickly, and, the administrative machinery there — if I may take the words of Mr. Malaisamy 
— is well oiled, and, therefore, administration fun ctions properly. In may States, where the 
administration does not have the will to act, where there is no political will to curb all these 
activities, the disturbances not only exist but also expand.  
Therefore, Sir, in this background, I thought to move this Resolution. Sir, several steps 
have been taken, particularly, by our hon. Home Minister who is heading the Consultative 
Committee on Home Affairs. During his tenure, several Consultative Committee meetings 
have been held regarding modernisation of police force and curbing the naxalite violence. 
They are even contemplating a police force on the lines of FBI in the State to look after the 
federal crime. Our Home Minister is personally interested in doing several things and solving 
the problem but the remedy lies somewhere else, to which I will come later.  
Sir, the Standing Committee of the Chief Ministers of seven naxalite-affected States has 
been formed under the chairmanship of the Home Secretary. Sir, a taskforce on inter-State 
coordination was constituted to review the implemen tation of the various programmes of 
the Central Government in naxalite-affected areas.  
Sir, meetings are held, discussions take place, dec isions are arrived at but when the 
question of implementation comes up, the problem arises because there is some defect in the 
delivery system. Because of-the deficiency in the d elivery system, the naxalite-affected 
States or Districts are not able to come out of the ir problems. This is the problem in the 
structure.  
Sir, the naxalite-movements are spreading in more a nd more States. The International 
Financial Services Company, Citigroup Inc. said tha t naxalite insurgency would not only 
hamper India's economic growth but also restrict the inflow of FDI into the country. There is 
another danger that growing unrest and continued de terioration in security levels in India 
coal heartland would have a significant impact on energy security in India and beyond.  
Sir, a report appreared that the Maoists are setting up regional, Zonal or State committees 
and special forces to target urban areas and towns.  Sir, this is a dangerous development 
which has taken place of late. Alarming warnings have been issued to industrial belts like 
Bhilai, Ranchi, Dhanbad, Kolkata; and also Mumbai, Pune, Surat, Ahmedabad seems to 
have been identified for urban mobilisation.  

Private Member's  [20 MARCH 2008]  Resolution 201  
Sir, as the Government of India plans several corri dors for connecting the roads and 
ports, naxalites are also having several corridors to link the urban belts and industrial belts 
for mobilising. This has to be taken care of. Several reports appear in papers that naxalites' 
activities have been curtailed; their supply chain has been cut. Several ideas are floated, 
several articles are written, suggestions are offered but, ultimately, Sir, it is spreading from 
State to State.  
Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the House towards the Status Report of the Home 
Ministry. Sir, in 2007, up to 30.06.2007, the numbe r of incidents, 842; police personnel 
killed, 138; civilians killed, 220; and Naxalites killed, 93. Sir, there is a comparative chart 
which says that in 2003, reported incidents were 1597; police personnel killed, 105; civilians 
killed, 410; and naxalites killed, 216.  
Sir, why am I comparing these figures? The statisti cs given will give us a statistical 
satisfaction that the incidents are less; the number of persons killed is less; and the number 
of police personnel killed is less. But the fact re mains, the violence, the movement still 
persists. That has to be taken care of.  
Sir, naxalism is not a law and order problem. That has been repeatedly told by the hon. 
Home Minister also. It has deep socio-economic dime nsions also. Sir, in this respect, the 
Home Ministry has given figures relating to naxal violence in Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, 
Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Maharashtra, etc. What are the steps that the Central Government 
is asking the State Governments to take to face the naxal violence?  
Sir, in 2007, till the end of June, there were 842 incidents of naxal violence and in the 
corresponding period in 2006, it was 827 incidents;  the number of police personnel and 
civilians killed was 358 against 396 in the corresponding period of 2006. Sir, in 2007, till 
the end of June, the number of police personnel killed was 138 and 220 civilians were killed 
as against 304 in the corresponding period of 2006. 
Sir, what support the Central Government is giving to the naxal-affected States is also 
found in the Status Report. Thirty-three battallions of the CPMF are currently deployed in 
anti-naxal duties in various States for assisting the State Police Forces. Twenty-nine Indian 
Reserve Battallions have been sanctioned for naxal-affected States. Fifteen battallions have 
been raised so far.  
Under the Scheme of Modernisation of State Police F orces, assistance for modern 
weaponry, latest communication equipment, mobility and other infrastructure is being 
provided. Naxal-affected States have also been asked to identify vulnerable police stations 
and outpost for fortification under the Scheme. Whether the naxal-affected States have done 
this is a question. I will come with an answer to it later.  
Sir, to upgrade the capability of the State Police Forces in weaponry, communication and 
handling of explosives, a special allocation of Rs.  100 crore was made under the Police 
Modernisation Scheme for seven naxal-affected States in 2006-07 in addition to the normal 
allocation. This is the extra money given by the Ho me Ministry.  
Security-related expenditure is also being reimbursed to the States. Sir, from February 
2005, it has been increased from 50 per cent to 100  per cent. Hundred per cent amount is 
reimbursed for rehabilitation, insurance scheme for police personnel, community policing 
and also for the expenditure which is incurred on publicity to counter the naxal propaganda 
and other security-related items. The Scheme is ext ended for five more years beyond 
31st March 2006.  

202   Private Member's  [RAJYASABHA]     Resolution  
Sir, 40 per cent of the recruitment in the Central Paramilitary Forces is provided to border 
areas and the areas affected by militancy and naxal ism. This is the Centre's contribution. 
These are some of the steps which are taken by the Central Government to help the naxal-
affected States, to augment their police forces, to modernise their police forces, to develop 
their equipment system, to develop the intelligence network, etc. Sir, on the developmental 
front, what has happened? Under the Backward Districts Initiatives, for the Rashtriya Sam 
Vikas Yojana, which covered 147 districts including 55 districts having Naxal-affected areas, 
amount of Rs. 45 crore per district had been allocated on a non-lapsable basis. Sir, in addition 
to the Backward Districts Initiative, the scheme of Backward Regions Grant Fund was initiated 
in 250 districts including around 107 districts having Naxal-affected areas. Sir, the the total 
provision for this is Rs. 25,000 crore during the E leventh Five Year Plan. For the current 
year, Sir, an amount of Rs. 4,670 crores is there which includes a component of Rs. 1 crore 
per district for capacity building. Sir, in additio n to all these things, special packages are 
given. Sir, the Government of India has given Rs. 1,000 crores to Bihar and Rs. 250 crores 
per year to Orissa. Sir, in addition to these speci al grants, the Government is also giving 
various schemes for the whole of India, particularl y for the Naxal-affected areas. For the 
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, there is an allocation of Rs. 6,000 crores in the current 
year. It is a wide opportunity to take up the rural connectivity on priority.  
Sir, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Progra mme in one of the flagship 
programmes of this Government, the UPA Government l ed by the Congress Party. They 
introduced it in 200 districts, extended to 330 dis tricts and now, this scheme is going to 
come into operation in the whole of India to give wage employment to the rural poor. Sir, the 
above scheme is in addition to the National Rural Health Scheme, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, 
Integrated Child Development Service Scheme, the schemes of the Ministries of Tribal Affairs, 
Social Welfare, Human Resource Develeopment, etc. A ll other Government Departments 
and Ministries are giving separate schemes for States.  
Therefore, Sir, the last step is to protect the tribals. Sir, to protect the tribal people from 
being evicted and harassed, this Government passed the Scheduled Tribes and Other 
Traditional Forest Dwellers Act, 2006. Sir, why I a m explaining all this is, in the last four 
years, this Government has increased the allocation for various social welfare schemes. Sir, 
this Government is trying to help the States withou t any discrimination, whether it is Biju 
Janata Dal in Orissa or BJP in one State or some ot her party in some other State. In Bihar, 
Shri Nitish Kumar is the Chief Minister. The Government has given Rs. 1000 crores to Bihar 
as a special package. So, this Government, without any discrimination, in national interest, 
in order to help the States, in order to overcome the difficulties faced by the States, in order 
to eliminate Naxalism and keep the States peaceful and in order to retrieve and rehabilitate 
the rural poor, introduced these schemes. Sir, if all these schemes are put together and if all 
the money which is spent by the Central Government on these schemes is put together and if 
any take a particular district, particularly the Naxal-affected district, I will say that heaven 
will come into that district. It will be a earthly heaven to live in those districts. Many crores 
of rupees are given for good roads, drinking water,  health scheme, wages, employment 
guarantee, education, old-age pension, etc. But, the question is: Whether the delivery system 
for all these schemes is correct or not? There lies  the problem. In spite of the fact that the 
money is being given and in spite of the two-pronged approach of the Home Minister, namely, 
to strengthen the police force and also the Government's intention to develop the area and to 
help the people in all respects for overall and accelerated growth, it is to be seen, whether it

happens. Unfortunately, Sir, It is not. Sir, I will cite what is happending at present. That is 
more important.  
Sir, there was an investigation, by the Indian Express, regarding Bihar to which a RS,

item which appeared in the newspaper on 25th February, 2008 is: "No electricity, no phone,

"The IG Operations, has blamed the State? Whom? The Finance Minister, for delaying the

these circumstances is a question that I want to put to the hon. Minister.

SHRI B.S. GNANADESIKAN: Sir, in the morning session, I was stating how the Central 
Government helps the Naxal-affected States with huge funds not only for the development 
of the region but also for augmenting and modernising the police forces, etc. I also pointed 
out how the delivery system is bad in these States and the beneficiaries have not been able to 
benefit from these schemes. Sir, to further strengt hen my argument on this score, I would 
like to quote a writer of an article in a magazine; he claimed that he had been touring all the 
Naxal-affected areas; he has written an article which has been published in a weekly magazine.  
According to him, in the tribal majority districts of KBK, that is, Kalahandi, Bolangir and 
Koraput, of Orissa, Rs. 2,000 crores, cumulatively spent, ostensibly on social welfare and 
rural development schemes during the past three years, has Just vanished. Nothing is there. 
He also says, "One of the reasons is that in the vast Central Indian highlands, an occasional 
visit of an official invariably means extraction by  coercion of whatever little the people 
have; it does not end with just a chicken or a goat or a bottle of mahua; if often includes all 
these and the modesty of the womenfolk. Most tribal villages and settlements have no access 
to schools and medical facilities. Very few are connected with all-weather roads. They have 
no electricity supply, though all the coalmines and  most of the hydel projects to generate 
power are in the tribal regions. The forests have been pillaged and the vergin forests, thick 
with giant sal trees are things of the past". Sir, this is the article written by that author who 
claims to have travelled throughout the Naxal-affected districts. He has written this article 
which was published in the magazine on 15th Februar y, 2008.  
Sir, there is a promise which has been made by Shri Laxmi Mittal to invest one lakh crore 
of rupees in Orissa and Jharkhand for starting a steel industry. According to the estimate, it 
will create, at least, a hundred thousand jobs directly and one to three million jobs indirectly. 
To get the raw material, that is, iron ore, he must have mine. If he wants mine, then the tribal 
people who are occupying the land will have to be displaced. There will be a resistance. One 
of the reasons, they say, is the amendment to the Mines and Minerals Act of 1957, providing 
for the power of acquisition of land for the purpos e of mining; so, one of the causes for 
displacement of people is the use of this power by the State Executive harshly without taking 
into consideration the human sentiments. The other consideration seems to be the introduction 
of, or, allowing, the foreign companies to enter into this politically-charged area for mineral 
development. These are the two reasons which they a ttribute to the growing unrest in the 
tribal area because the Land Acquisition Act, which is very harsh, displaces a person. The 
house is built with the hard-earned money and, subsequently, when compulsory acquisition 
takes place, for whatever reason, either for private purpose or on the request of a company 
or for public purpose by the Government, ultimately , the person looses his house. The 
compensation given by the Government does not substitute the structure or the house which 
he has built or the land which he possesses. There are also sentiments attached to the house

and to the land he owns. Therefore, one of the suggestions—again quoting the Mittal steel plant-is 
that by establishing a steel plant in Orissa, Chhat tisgarh or Jharkhand, Rs. 70,000 crores of 
revenue will be created. And half a per cent of that, in perpetuity, if it is given to the sufferers who 
have lost their land or the building, they will bec ome rich; their children can be educated. 
Therefore, they will not only be adequately compensated but also sufficiently compensated. More 
than the compensation, they will have a peaceful li fe because of the money power which they 
possess. The idea is, these persons must be made as a partners, the person who loses the land or the 
house must be made as a partner in the developmenta l projects so that they will become a partner 
of the scheme, and they would not have a feeling that their land or their house has been taken away 
forcibly by the use of this Act, the Land Acquisition Act or whatever Act. Therefore, Sir, these are 
the two aspects which I would like to put forth for the overall consideration of the government.

Status Paper issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs  as on January I, 2008. Sir, I would like to

component for strengthening of intelligence set up. 
This is the status of the States' request.  
Sir, the other aspect is, under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme, which 
was operationalised for 20 districts initially, in September, 2005, Rs. 10,025.95 crores released in 
2005-06 and 2006-07 but the total utilisation by An dhra Pradesh, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, 
Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal was only Rs. 
6,018.38 crores. Therefore, even the amount which w as given under the scheme, they were not 
able to utilise. In 2007-08, Rs. 7,060.67 crores have been released under the NREGP.  
Sir, coming to the police force—I was explaining ho w the two police stations in Bihar 
were situated in spite of several crores of rupees pumped in for modernisation, 100 per cent 
reimbursement, etc.—I would further like to say thi s. In Andhra Pradesh, the vacancy position 
was 7.27 per cent. That is tolerable, Sir. In Bihar , the vacancy position is 28.91 per cent. 
There are 16,223 officers, 68,115 men; totalling 84 ,338, but only 24,384 are available. The 
percentage is 28.91 per cent; this is the shortage.  This is the vacancy position. In Chhattisgarh, 
there are 4,218 officers, 31,257 men; totalling 35, 475. The shortage is 7,641, which is 21.54 
per cent. Similarly, in Jharkhand, which is the most affected State,—both Chhattisgarh and   
Jharkhand—there are 31,225 vacancies. It is 24.26 p er cent. As far as Madhya Pradesh is 
concerned, it is 5.42 per cent, which is tolerable.  Maharashtra figure is also tolerable with 
7.13 per cent. Again, Orissa, another most naxal-affected State, is at 21.24 per cent—namely,   
10,417 vacancies exist in the police force. Similarly, West Bengal with 9.3 per cent is tolerable. This 
hon. House may take into account the vacancy position. I am repeating, in spite of all the sincere 
efforts taken by the Union as well as the Home Minister, they are not able to fill

up the existing vacancies in the police force, forget about the creation of additional posts in 
the police force. They are not able to fill up even the existing vacancies.  
Sir, one interesting factor which comes under the Status Report is the number of kilometres 
one police station covers. That is more important. In Andhra Pradesh, the total area covered 
by one police station is 168.22 square kilometres. I am not reading the figures of all States. 
In Chhattisgarh, one police station has to cover 440.36 square kilometres. Then, how do you 
expect the police stations to be more effective in containing the naxal movement? It is humanly 
impossible. Similarly, in Madhya Pradesh, one polic e station has to cover 333.6 square 
kilometres. In Orissa, one police station has to co ver 335.58 square kilometres. Therefore, 
unless the shortcomings of filling up of existing vacancies in police force is taken care, reducing 
the quantum of square kilometres which a police station can cover is a distant reality.  
Then, creation of additional police force in which the Central Government assists, making 
utilisation of all schemes which the Central Govern ment offers like hundred per cent 
reimbursement of security-related items, utilisation of all the social sector welfare schemes 
launched by this Government reaching the beneficiary, creation of all weather roads, water 
supply, jobs, old-age pension, good health, if these common ends are properly done by the 
State Government, then only, I think, this problem can be overcome.  
Sir, I will take only a few minutes. The structure of the naxal movement is improving. 
According to one newspaper report, they are having a central military commission also. 
They are also having military intelligence and cent ral instructors' team. Interestingly, Sir, 
when we are presenting the Budget in the Parliament , they are also presenting a budget of 
Rs. 60 crores for 2000-2008. Sir, this is a very serious issue.  
They have a separate team for arms and ammunitions. Naxal incidents are not remote and 
isolated incidents. Now-a-days, the naxalites are not drawn by dogmas or issues of any anti-
wealth or anti-landlord psyche. They are only exploiting the tribals and the poor people for 
whom the benefits have not reached because of non-governance in certain areas by the State 
Governments. That is the reason why these naxals are able to exploit and recruit people for 
naxal movement. Therefore, the basic difference on how the naxal movement started earlier, 
how people were attracted because of ideology and dogmas, how they have a policy, is no 
more there. Now, it is like a structured organisation spreading through a well-oiled-machinery 
like a government machinery. Though our Government is taking all-out efforts, it is the 
responsibility of the State Governments to take care of all these things.  
Sir, even they have collected 'protection money'. I was told that the intelligence agencies 
have listed some 120 mining companies and crusher units who have paid more than Rs. 12 
crores for protecting their industry. They have developed a central technical unit in Jharkhand, 
including a mobile van, to repair their weapons and to develop explosives. Sir, these are the 
things, which are required to be attended to not by  the Government or the Home Ministry 
but by the State Governments concerned. Sir, the sp read of Naxalism is an indication of 
desperation and alienation among a large section of  the nation. They have not only been 
systematically marginalised but also cruelly exploi ted and dispossessed of their last 
homelands. Therefore, Sir, all these things should be taken care of by the State Governments 
and if the money in crores that flows through these schemes reaches the beneficiaries, there 
will be magical transformation in the Naxal areas. People will lead a peaceful, happy life; 
children will go for education, old age people will  get pension, rural people will get 
employment and healthcare. There should be a corruption-free implementation of the scheme

at the State level. There should not be diversification of money to other areas. There should

corresponding obligation. Therefore, the Committee feels, the CBI with appropriate stature 
and backing .suo motu cognises the crimes, which in no way affect the ess entials of our

suggested is that the CBI can take suo motu action against the crimes in the States. That is

regularly interacting with the Chief Ministers of t he Naxal affected States and he is also 
trying, as best as possible, to help the States whichever party is power in those States. But, 
ultimately, Sir, it is for the States to take advan tage of the lending help. That is the reason 
why I made this Resolution to request for the respo nsibility and accountability by the 
Government of India by making necessary amendments so that delivery is overhauled. As a 
responsive Central Government, it can see the funds  allotted for the schemes reach the 
destination. Sir, any pillage, corruption official or political must be dealt with an iron hand. 
The good governance in the worst of law and order environment is the need of the hour. The 
best civilian administrative structure must come up  in place of total non-governance. 
Therefore, Sir, part (e), (f) and (g) of my Resolution is to be taken note of by the Government.

of our Jawans who are guarding our frontiers and police forces guarding our internal security 
should be taken care of. They are working in onerous conditions. The boys are to be educated 
and girls to be married, old parents are to be looked after. Therefore, they also deserve our

uniform, who by their belief act inhumanly with a w ooden heart. They must be identified 
and shifted. These measures are the need of the hour. Sir, during my student days, 40 years 
back, there was some agitation in Coimbatore when I was in college. When we were agitating,

whenever there was agitation. So, when the students started emotionally pelting stones, the 
Collector who was standing with the police rushed to the students' side and he also picked up 
one stone and pretended as though he was also with the students throwing the stones on the

SHRISHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, I stand here to support the Resolution 
moved by my friend and colleague, Shri B. S. Gnanadesikan. At the outset, I would like to 
touch upon an important suggestion made by my colleague with respect to an amendment in 
the Constitution for tackling the problems in distr icts which are affected by naxalites. I 
would suggest by adding to his suggestion that such districts, for a temporary period of say 
five years or so can be declared as deemed Union Territories whereby the Administration of 
the district can be taken over by the Central Gover nment, funds can be provided, all help 
can be given and appropriate law and order machiner y can be installed there so that peace 
and calm is restored over a period of time. Apart f rom that, social and development aspect 
can also be looked after.  
Sir, it is said that Naxalite movements originate b asically because of poverty. But, the 
poor necessarily are not violent. One cannot say th at poverty per se leads to concept like 
naxalism. There are some administrative matters which, coupled with poverty, lead to such 
type of movements. This is my humble opinion. For i nstance, if a Government authority 
gives certain benefits to the poor people and when a poor person approaches the authority to 
seek that relief, and if he is not treated properly  there, it is that anger which leads to these 
types of movements, but not poverty per se. If a person goes to obtain a loan and if he is not 
treated properly, if he is made to visit the concerned office again and again, it is that anger 
which causes naxalism. If a person goes to obtain a ration card, for which he has to report ten 
times to the office of Tehsildar and he is not issued one, it is this type of negligence on the 
part of authorities towards the poor which leads to  such things. It is not merely the empty 
stomach of our poor people; they can tolerate hunge r, but they cannot, obviously, tolerate 
insult of this type meted out to them. Again, in th e matter of health, when they go to the 
primary health centres, when their dear ones suffer due to negligence of doctors and health 
workers, then, these things lead to anger in poor people. Therefore, we have also to see that 
legal machinery, the administrative machinery, is i mprovised. We have to make our laws 
simple because, ultimately, we are governed by our laws. Even if some reliefs are given, 
everything is governed by a legal system. We have to simplify the laws and I would suggest 
that a Committee should be appointed to study all the Central legislations and State legislations 
which deal with common man's day-to-day affairs. It should study and recommend simplified 
procedures in those legislations so that justice is  done to those who seek relief on such 
issues. Similar is the case of Government schemes. Thousands of schemes of State Government 
and Central Government are there. In fact, these schemes regulate the regular life of weaker 
sections of our society. These schemes, and not the legislations, govern their lives. We should 
make these schemes simplified so that anybody seeki ng relief under these schemes is not 
harassed by any Government officer.  
As far as naxalite movement is concerned, although it originated in West Bengal but, 
today, Andhra Pradesh is considered to be the fortress of this movement. If I am not mistaken,  
9 out of 23 districts in Andhra Pradesh are now affected by it. There is an analysis made in 
which it is said that merger of PWG and MCC in 2004 to form the Communist Party of India 
(Maoists) is seen as a significant development in t he armed rebellion within the country, 
merger marks a new phase in the naxal movement. Rig ht now, 19 out of 23 districts of 
Andhra Pradesh are under declared naxal infested Districts. In these areas, the organisational 
structure of the CPI (Maoist) includes six military  platoons, 28 area committees, 66 local 
guerrilla squads and 16 action teams. There are three Special Zonal Committees in  

Private Member's  [20 MARCH 2008]  Resolution   217

called the CPI (Maoist) State Committee. This is the administrative set up of this movement.

care of, there is a very, very less scope for indulging in such activities. So, slowly, the problems 
are getting eradicated.  
Sir, in the State of Tamil Nadu, we have made the basic education free, and the students 
who are coming from distant villages are given bicycles. So, the transportation is also free. 
They use the bicycles. The Central Government is al so funding that project. 1 myself had 
gone to several schools to distribute bicycles to the girls and boys studying in those schools.  
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): It is launched by the State Government.  
SHRI SHUNMUGASUNDARAM: The State Government has lau nched this scheme, 
but it is a Central Government-funded scheme. Sir, these are the measures taken by the 
Government. At the same time, education is also given. Through the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
scheme, education is now being imparted to the masses, and now the human resources of the 
country are slowly converted into assets. The liter acy rate is going up. Sir, these are all 
measures that will help in eradicating the Naxalite violence. But, at the same time, Sir, the 
police forces and the paramilitary forces are now empowered, under the law, to take stringent 
measures, and the Government will also support them , for preventing these activities. Sir, 
the Government should be cautious about one aspect. There is a criticism — I don't want to 
specify any place—being made all over the country t hat there are several encounter deaths 
taking place. Sir, in these encounter deaths, the police shoot out various suspects. This further 
angers some of these groups. Sir, false cases are foisted on them. In some cases, they dont' 
stand in court. We have been, Sir, in cases relating to the forest brigand Veerappan that about 
125 or 130 persons were prosecuted for terrorism charges. I happened to go and see them in 
the prison. I went to the special courts, the desig nated courts, in Bangalore. Many of them 
were women and elderly people. They were all acquit ted Except four or five, all of them 
were acquitted. There were several cases filed agai nst them. They were forced to face the 
trial. At that time, they informed that there were indiscriminate killings in shoot-outs by the 
police. This has also to be looked into by the Government. The encounter killings should not 
be carried out indiscriminately. An inquiry into the encounter killings should not be an eye-
wash inquiry because that will only incite the peop le further and complicate the problem 
further. This Naxalite problem is now becoming a transnational problem. It has become an 
international problem. Our neighbouring country is also facing this problem. It is spreading 
from the neighbouring country as well as from the groups here to other places. (Time-bell). 
So, the international police force should be activated. How much more time do I have, Sir?  

220 Private Member's  [RAJYA SABHA]  Resolution  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): Two minutes.  
SHRI R. SHUNMUGASUNDARAM: Thank you. Sir, there are unemployed people on 
the road-side. In the heart of those unemployed people, who are on the road-side, dangerous 
ideas crop up. That is the danger of the society. T hat is what our leader said. It is very 
relevant to the topic which we are discussing now. I congratulate Mr. Gnanadesikan and 
support the Resolution also. With these words, I conclude. Thank you.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): You have ten minutes' time.  
DR. K. KESHAVARAO (Andhra Pradesh): I was told that I would be given 15-20 minutes.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P. J. KURIEN): You take te n minutes. The Home 
Minister has to reply after that, and we have to finish it by 4 o' clock.  
DR. K. KESHAVA RAO: Sir, I would like to co-operate with you; I would rather not speak 
at all and allow the Home Minister to speak, because when I am speaking, all of us seem to 
have a common perspective instead of different perspectives on this issue. Let me tell you, 
how we look into the problem is important. I totally agree with the sentiments expressed by 
my friends. All of us are against violence. Not to be mistaken, let me start my sentence, with 
all emphasis and coming from the core of my heart, that I am a pacifist; I am against violence. 
I believe that violence has no place in democracy, But what is the 'democracy and what is the 
society which you are talking about? And what kind of a violence are you trying to talk? If I 
go to a village for voting, a landlord or a feudal lord can stop me, looking high at me and 
raising his eye-brow, that is not violence to you! If somebody uses his lathi and sends me 
and my family out of my village, and cast all the v otes by himself, that is not violence for 
you. If I have to criticise the BJP for something w rong, I have to take up some kind of an 
issue so that I browbeat them, or they take up some kind of an issue through which they can 
browbeat me, that is not a political rivalry. But if a particular person, takes the real situation 
of the society today, — after sixty years, the kind  of reality that we have — where 36 
families hold the entire wealth of the nation, and 72-75 per cent of people live with Rs. 20 a 
day, then, you will know what and why of violence. Only this morning, you were trying to 
talk about a postman getting Rs. 1800 a month with four people to support, which means he 
gets less than Rs. 14 per day. If that is the kind of condition, and you would like to say, and 
everybody says, /dvletterma/dvletterra/dvletterta/dvvowelsignaa /g175/dvletterya/dvvowelsignaa /dvletterna/uni0939/g530 /dvletterka/dvletterra/dvletterta/dvvowelsignaaि " that means you are supporting it. Everybody says, 
what would happen? If the situation is this, why don't we go away and rebel? That means all 
of you know that the condition is bad, there is no alternative but to get into some kind of a 
violent activity. It is only violence that has been  creating,this situation. I am not trying to 
support Maoism or the thousand flowers that may blo ssom, nor am I trying to support the 
"swarm attack" way back at Jehanabad. We have had many swarm attacks after Jehanabad; 
550 to be very precise, and all with success. Only last month, we had it in Orissa, from where 
1600 arms were taken away. So, what I am trying to tell you is that this issue needs a very 
serious attention and consideration. It is not that the Home Ministry is not looking into it. I 
know that the Home Minister is doing that. The other day, when he was speaking, I was so 
much impressed. But is he solving it? Shri Gnanades ikan was quoting all the papers. The 
heading is, "Naxalism feeds on genuine issues—It ca lls for policy not police." Quoting this, 
he wants the police to take the centre-stage. Then, he wanted to quote Mohan Guruswamy to 
say that there are several paradoxes to be dealt with, but the most important one is how to  

222 Private Member's  [RAJYA SABHA]  Resolution  
provide.good governance in the worst of law and order situation. A better civil administration structure 
must come up in place of the one that I am talking by violence and populist sanction. They are saying 
the same thing, asking for the help of the police. 1 am not saying that police should not come in. I 
would only like to tell you, for a minute, the success story of Andhra Pradesh. How did we do it? 
Sir, Andhra suffered it for the last 40 years. But it is only the last four years that we do not have that 
kind of a thing. I am not saying that Naxalism has been totally rooted out. Why do we treat 
Naxalism as a menace? At the same time, say: *TOTT 3RT Tiff «RtH? But it is a menace to you. I 
have not been able to understand the jargon in this. First of all, let us understand rural activism. 
Having seen the tribal areas, this came as a crop-sharing issue in Naxalbari. I am not going into the 
history at all. I am saying about the success story of Andhra Pradesh. When we called them for 
discussions, eye-brows were raised here in the Home Ministry at the Centre. They thought, how 
the Naxalities, who do not believe in elections, electoral politics, who do not believe in elected 
Governments, would come for talks. We need to have persuasive methods. When I was talking to 
Nirmala Behan, when I was trying to take out what was known as Shanti Yatra, when our talks, I 
went directly into their dens, as you call it, which I call their centres. I went to their centres in 16 
districts. There was no violence there. The next day, they came to the table to have discussions 
with us. What was the conditionally when we invited them to talks? I am just making a reference. 
The earlier Government had said, "You give up your arras and then come for talks". They had 
refused. We said, "Whatever you want to talk, please come; even the giving up of arms can be 
discussed". We put it in the agenda. Believe me, they just came dropping their guns and entered 
the hall. For six months thereafter, we had a lull. We could have continued further but for very 
wrong happenings over which we really brooded over the things and found out what exactly we 
needed to do. That is a very specific issue. But I am not going back into why it has all come. The 
more perlexing paradox of today is that every one of us here believe that Naxalism is some kind 
of a socio-economic problem. Every gentleman who spoke here said this. Yet, after speaking of 
that, first they talked about the modernisation of police, about the battalions being sent to the 
States, the States being empowered, the money flowing into the States to fortify the police 
stations and so on. All this is all right. To cut the story short, let me tell you, we should have a three-
pronged approach which the horn Home Minister mentioned the other day. We need to be stern. 
We need to handle it very sternly. But, understand the sensitivity of the issue, the sensitivity of 
the milieu in which people live, the poor man lives, with practically nothing at all and with the 
vulgarity of the wealth that you have in your hands, with your TVs and other things shown to us 
through your showcases. This is how we have to do it. Number one is, never talk about the police 
forces; never talk about how many battalions you are sending, what kind of modernisation of the 
police you are doing, what kind of new materials you are giving, what kind of technology you 
are putting in the police stations and so on. Do it; it is your job to do it. Nobody is stopping you 
from doing it. But you need not put all the bravado to that. What is needed to be done? You talk 
about remote area's development, about the panchayati raj. Although the panchayati raj started and 
has failed there. Where is the Gram Sabha today? You all talk about the Gram Sabha! The feudal raj 
and the big man who has always being dictating to us can still go and get all the things done. Can 
anybody dare get up and stand against him and say 'no' to him? Things are changing. I am not being 
cynical at all, Sir. Things are changing. Till then, we need to adjust ourselves and blend ourselves 
with the changing milieu. Then, what is to be done? Sir, panchayati raj is one revolutionary step 
that we have taken in this country since we have had our independence where you try to take the 
spirit of democracy, if not democracy, the sense of humanism, if not humanity, to the people. 
Tell them, here is  

Private Member's  [20 MARCH 2008]  Resolution   223  
 
 
your power, if you want to use it. What is it that we have done to strengthen those sinews? 
Nothing. So, what I am saying is, talk about what you could do, say, for the development of 
that remote area. Now, what we have done is we have  recruited Home Guards in Andhra 
Pradesh. Three lakh Home Guards in tribal areas! Fi rstly, this has provided a sort of 
employment to people. Then, within two years, we have distributed 4.5 lakh acres of land. 
That is because wherever these Naxals go, they talk about land as the major issue. Sir, let me 
tell you, when the Naxalites had come for talks and they were talking about land, I had just 
turned back to one of them and asked, in the presence of all, "What is your age? When you 
were not born, when Maoism was not born, or, even t he Maoist Party was not born, way 
back in 1942, Mahatma Gandhi was asked by Fishcher as to what should the agenda for the 
new, independent India be and he had said, "Land to the tiller". So, it has been an article of 
faith with this country, with this nation, let alon e the Congress Party. The Father of the 
Nation had said it. That is why I was hurt when Mr.  Gnanadesikan was saying why we 
shouldn't have an FBI style of operations or a CBI style of functioning or an Interpol type of 
functioning. Why not a Budha style of approach? Whe n King Ashoka decided, everybody 
followed him on the path of non-violence. Why not, say, Acharya Vinboa Bhave style of 
functioning? Why don't you say Mahatma Gandhi's style of functioning? Why don't you say 
Jai Prakash Narain's style of functioning? This is how you must win them over. So, my three-
pronged approach, on which I am trying to stress is this. I am not going into the history of 
Naxalism, but, if I go into the history, then, all of us will be hanging our heads in shame. We

after fifteen days' time. There is no point. I have made all the points which I wanted to make. I 
don't have to say anything more than this-. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Now, Shri Gn anadesikan. Now, Mr. 
Gnanadesikan, what I would suggest to you is that if you what to speak, then we can continue 
with this Resolution next time.  
SHRI B. GNANADESIKAN: Sir, only two minutes, please.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Then, you can speak next time.  
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, I will make a formal request to him to withdraw it. All the points 
which he has made are relevant. They are under our consideration. We have already taken 
decisions on those things ...(Interruptions)...  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): That's enough. So, Mr. Gnanadesikan, are 
you withdrawing the Resolution?  
SHRI B.S.GNANADESIKAN: Yes; Sir, I am withdrawing.  
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIEN): Ok, Does he have the permission of the 
House to withdraw the Resolutior?  
The Resolution was by leave withdrawn  
[MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair]  
FELICITATIONS TO THE RETIRING MEMBERS  
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members todays we bid farewell to some of our colleagues who are 
retiring this year on completion of their term of office. In the constitutional scheme of things, as 
you know, one-third of our Members retire every second year. This ensures continuity along with 
change in the composition of the House. Out of the 73 Members retiring this year, 57 Members will 
be completing their term of office in the months of April and May.  
Some of the retiring Members, I am sure, would be re-elected. Those who will not come back 
will certainly be missed by the House. The membership of the Rajya Sabha is in itself a great 
honour. Many of the retiring Members are public figures of standing, are well-versed in debating 
skills and in the art of criticising political opponents without offending them. Dignified debate is 
essential to democracy and is the finest form of communication. I place on record my heartfeit 
appreciation of the valuable contribution that the retiring Members have made to the deliberations 
of the House and the service they have rendered to parliamentary democracy. On a personal note, 
I am grateful for the consideration they have shown towards me in conducting the business of the 
House. I am sure that the Members who are retiring would cherish the memory of their association 
with this august House. I wish them good health, happiness, success and long years of service to 
the nation.  
Now, the hon. Leader of the Opposition.

Felicitation to the  [20 MARCH 2008]  Retiring Members 235  
SHRISITARAM YECHURY (West Bengal): Sir, this is indeed a very emotional moment. It is 
always very sad to say goodbye to your colleagues with whom you have woriced. For me, this is 
my first farewell speech that I am making in this august House. So, I am one of the most junior ones. 
Many of those, who are retiring, have been very senior to me in this House. They have contributed a 
lot and, personally, I am indebted to many tJC them for having; shown me the way in this House, 
when I was a newcomer, how to proceed ahead. And, I feel, all of us will be missing my brother, 
Shri Suresh Pachouri, who has been ably handling the delicate situation of how to keep the outside 
support inside and had been playing rather tedious role; Mr. Poojary, who was with me in our 
Standing Committee meetings; Madam Cariappa with whom I represented the Indian Parliament in 
one of our international meetings at the UNESCO.  
Mr. Ved Prakash Goyal and Mr. Shatrughan Sinha — unfortunately both of them are not here — 
both of them held the same portfolios and served in the same Standing Committee and were of 
great help and assistance in the functioning of that. They all will be missed here, particularly, my 
dear friend, Prof. Ram Deo Bhandary ji, with whom, I remember, many-many years ago, as a 
junior I used to accompany him in the helicopters in the campaign in Bihar and also when he 
was Leader of his Party in this House.  
Sir, Ravula Chandra Sekar Reddy and Become from the same State, and, he has been senior 
here. Sir, it is indeed very difficult to say goodbye to all such people. It is always with a fond hope 
that this is not saying goodbye to politics but to the membership of this House, as we are sure, 
they all will either come back here or interact with us in some way or the other.  
But Dr. P.C. Alexander told me that he has decided to call it quits; we will miss him surely. 
I, though much junior to him, told him, Sir, this is a great virtue if you are able to know when to 
leave and when not to come back again. I think, he has displayed this wisdom and is saying that 
he is not coming back.  
Sir, on behalf of the CPI (M), I would like to thank all of them for the cooperation that they 
have extended to us. There have been occasions, there will be occasions when from the political 
point of view, we may differ, we may contest each other, but, I think, that is the essence of 
democracy and that is the spirit of democracy that let the hundred flowers bloom, let a thousand 
thoughts contend, and, that is when we will have the best that this system can provide. So, I wish 
them success in their future with the fond hope that they will come back again to this House 
again, and, maybe, give a farewell speech when I retire. By that time, some of them will be here. 
With this, personally as well as on behalf of my party, I extend my best wishes for the future of 
all of them. Thank you.  
DR. V. MAITREYAN (Tamil Nadu): It is a moment of gratitude and sorrow, it is an occasion 
for gratitude because we remember the immense contribution made by the Members in enriching and 
elevating the quality of debate in this House. We remember them for the role that they play in 
diffusing the situation when the House witnesses turbulent situation. We remember them for 
adding wit and life in the functioning of the House. It is a moment of  

236    Felicitation to the  [RAJYASABHA]  Retiring Members  
sorrow because we will be missing them, especially, Suresh Pachouriji, with whom I had a 
very personal acquaintance and relationship, Prof. Ram Deo Bhandaryji, Shri Ravula Chandra 
Sekar Reddy, who is my left hand and Dr. PC. Alexander and others. I particularly remember, 
Dr. Alexander wrote a wonderful article just before the Session started. When I met him here 
in the corridors, I appreciated his article and I assured him that we will do exactly the opposite 
in the House. On this occasion, today, I assure you , Sir, we will definitely get the sense of 
your article and we will try to be good boys in the House.  
It is good to see quite a number of retiring Members to be back again in this House. As 
many as 17 members are returning back to this House. For Members of my Party and others 
from the regional parties, who are retiring today, it is a special occasion. Coming from far 
off places, with a totally new environment, with di fficulties in the language adjustments, 
they have adjusted themselves to the new environment, and, they did there very best in the

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Sir. I am 
thankful to you all the Members of this august House for all the support extended to me.  
Sir, I come from a remote village. I reached the Parliament from the Panchayat. I served 
the Andhra Pradesh Assembly for five years. I served this august House for six years. 1 have 
learnt many things from here. I am grateful to my party founder, Dr. N.T.R., who taught us 
self-respect. I am thankful to my leader, Mr. Chandrababu Naidu, who encouraged me and 
helped to develop self-confidence. I am particularly thankful to all party leaders. I am also 
thankful to all the Presiding Officers starting from late Krishan Kantji, Shekhawatji and you. 
I am also grateful to Rahman Sahib. I can't forget his broad smile. I am thankful to all the 
leaders of various political parties, especially, Sushmaji.  
1 have only one regret. We thought that during our tenure the Women Reservation Bill 
would be passed. But it was not. I request the hon. Prime Minister, at least, to see to it that

the Women Reservation Bill is passed in the coming days. We have been pleading for its 
passing for many years.  
The second point is the most painful thing of farmers' suicide. It is still on the rise. Apart 
from the steps taken by the Government, I think that some more steps need to be taken in 
future so that farmers' suicide can be stopped.  
The third, and the most important, point is recogni sing my mother tongue, Telugu, 
as a Classical language. We have been pleading, we have been agitating, for a long 
time. 1 can only request the Government; I can't demand since I am leaving the House. 
I request the Prime Minister to see to it that Telu gu is recognised as a Classical 
Language.  
Finally, I thank everybody in this august House. I thank the Secretary-General and 
all the officers and the Watch and Ward of this House. 1 am thankful to everybody.

that retirement is inevitable to everybody. Therefo re, retiring from this House does not 
mean that the work is over. In fact, my experience is that whenever you retire from 
one House, you always get a promotion. Therefore, S hri Pachouri need not worry 
about it. If somebody retires from this House, some times, he becomes a member of 
Lok Sabha, and, sometimes, he becomes the Speaker o f Lok Sabha. Therefore, nobody 
should worry about retirement. In fact, I honestly feel that there is a lot of work which

Chief Secretary and asked, 'What is the percentage of non-corrupt officers in the 
Government?" The Chief Secretary said, "Sir, the Ch ief Minister was wrong in telling 
you that 50 per cent of the officers are non-corrup t. The number is more." Dr.

Shri Ravula Chandra Sekar Reddy is also a thorough gentleman. In this House, I have seen 
that the people are extremely good. They are very n ice, well-behaved, before the House 
starts. Otherwise, they are all good friends. Therefore, I wish everybody, retiring today, all 
success in life. I have nothing more to add. But, s ometimes, I really feel whether it is 
necessary to be in politics for serving the society. I am not sure that those who may not be 
able to come to the House back—there may be constra ints for their leaders—they can do 
social work better outside than coming to the House . Therefore, my good wishes to 
everybody and thanks to everybody.  
DR. BIMAL JALAN (Nominated): Sir, I do not want to take too much of your time at this 
stage except to add my voice as well as that of my colleagues on this Bench of Nominated 
Members, who do not have a party affiliation, to share the thoughts-in the words of appreciation  

244 Felicitation to the  [RAJYA SABHA]  Retiring Members  
which have been expressed for those who are leaving the House. From a non-party perspective, 
the only point that I want to make is that irrespective of whichever party they belong, either 
on this side or that side—some who were on the othe r side are on this side now and similarly 
those who were on this side are on the other side n ow—some of the brightest people from 
different walks of life are in this House. Now, getting here is not easy. The numbers are few; 
we do not realise how few they are. There are only around 800 Members in the Houses of 
Parliament from the whole country of 100 crore peop le. So, to get here from any party 
perspective, from the bottom to this high level, is  not easy. And you can see this in the 
interventions, in their commitment to the party ideology, party programmes, but above all, 
to the commitment to our country's good. Sir, I wou ld like to bring to your notice, which I 
had not realised, that I had participated in the fu nctioning of this House in some way from 
that corner as well as appeared before several Standing Committees, in particular. What has 
struck me the most is the work of the Standing Committees. And I would like to put it that 
this is irrespective of whichever party the experts  and the brightest of our land belong to. 
Whenever any matter comes before a Standing Committ ee, one cannot imagine and one 
cannot see which party they belong to because what they are worried about and what they 
are thinking about is just the subject itself.  
Now, some of those who are retiring will not be coming back and they have been mentioned, 
like Mr. Pachouri and Mr. Poojary with whom I have worked. I have appreciated their kindness 
to us. And, of course, there is the iconic figure o f Dr. Alexander who has contributed so 
much in so many different walks of life.  
I just want to tell you that it has been a privilege for us to watch the people work, and of 
those who are leaving, I do not really think they are leaving. If they do not come back here, 
they are, I am absolutely sure, going to continue to serve the country in whatever walk of life 
they come from.  
I just take this opportunity to convey the best wis hes of all of us from this side of the 
House. Thank you very much.  
SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, this is my third session of the Parliament. 
In that way, I am the junior most to bid farewell to our retiring Members. Sir, I have known 
many of them outside the Parliament earlier and my beloved brother, Shri Suresh Pachouri 
was one of the leaders of the Youth Congress, and I  was the General Secretary of the All 
India Youth federation. We had worked together on m any issues. We had participated in 
many international and national events. After coming to parliament, I could watch him work 
and also watch the work being done by other hon. members. In this short period I did learn 
a lot from them, like how to conduct oneself in Parliament, how to comprehend issues, how 
to take up the cause of the people relentlessly. In  that respect, I owe my gratitude to these 
Members.  
For a political activist, retirement is only notional. For a political activist, work goes on. 
His service to the people and his service for the country continues and it will continue.  
On behalf of CPI, I join the entire House in wishing them all the best and all success in the 
coming years. Thank you very much, Sir.  
SHRI TIRUCHI SIVA (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman, Sir, parting is always painful. Some 
unpleasant moments like these, which everyone wants to avoid, do come across in our lives. 
There is a saying 'we meet, we know, we love, only to part'. But I am sure that we will feel 
proud in the days to come when we recollect that these retiring Members were our colleagues  

Felicitation to the  [20 MARCH 2008]  Retiring Members 245  
in this august House. The debates in which they par ticipated, the deliberations they made, 
did reflect their vast experience and broad-wisdom. Their prudence added glory to the dignity, 
of this august House.  
Sir, we are all from various political parties of d ifferent ideologies. These differences 
might have designed our manner of discussions, but they have never altered the goal of our 
mission, that is, the nation's interest, the thin t hread which binds all of us from various 
quarters of our country. And this spirit was upheld to the best by all these retiring Members 
during their days here.  
I would like to specially mention here that Shri Shanmugasundaram who is retiring as a 
Member of this House from our Party, came to my place in 2002.I had the same experience 
at that time. He served as the Floor Leader of our Party here. Then, I have seen Shri Suresh 
Pachouri on the other side in those days. His loud voice had been missing all these days, 
after he had become the Minister. We will miss him in the days to come. This is a very sad 
aspect that we have to accept. So also about Shrijanardhana Poojary about whom I should 
mention that he is a person who appreciates and enc ourages people like us whenever they 
participate in a debate and make speeches.  
All the Members here, especially, my dear friend, Shri Ajay Maroo and Shri Shatrughan 
Sinha from the BJP, though they are from the Opposition side, all along, they have been our 
good friends. Sir, we will be missing Janab Syed, Mr. Perumal, Bhandaryji, Premaji and so 
many other Members. I congratulate them all for the ir extra-ordinary and remarkable 
performance in this House. I thank them for their a ffection, and I wish them all success in 
their future endeavour. Sir, one thing, I must say that we will miss them in the days to come. 
Thank you very much, Sir.

Felicitation to the  [20 MARCH 2008]  Retiring Members 247  
SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): *Hon'ble Chairman, We have come to a moment of 
thanksgiving. Every meeting comes to an end with the proposal of vote of thanks. I presume 
similar thing is taking place at this sweeter momen t. When it comes to politics and public 
life there is very little meaning for the work 'rest'. There can be a respite to a term in Parliament 
or Legislative Assembly. But in public life there i s no rest or respite. This is my avowed 
view.  
I would like to putforth certain view points here. As a global citizen. I would like to identify 
myself as an Indian. As an Indian citizen, I would like to identify myself as a Tamilian. At this 
moment, I would like to recall some people to whom I owe much in life. Maatha, Pitha, Guru, 
Dei van are the four. Mother, Father, Teacher and God are the four that form a core in our lives.  
In Tamil literature, in the early Sangam literature a poetess by name Penmudiar has written 
a poem worth quoting here on this occasion.  
'Eendru purantharuthal en thalai kadaney.  
Sandron aakkuthal thanthaikku kadaney.  
Vel vadithu koduththal kollarkku kadaney'  
[Giving birth to and bringing us up is the duty of a mother, Shaping him up to be a scholar 
is the duty of a father, Providing him with spear to establish him is the duty of a smith.]  
A mother gives shape to a man by giving birth to hi m. A father gives shape to a man 
shaping him up to be a scholar. But he is shaped to be a human being by the society he lives 
in. He becomes good or bad or a useful man by the forces wielded by the society.  
My mother gave me life as a man and gave me a good childhood and upbringing. My 
father also enabled me to grow as a well educated man. It is this society that has shaped me 
up to be what I am now. I would like to refer as 'Society' our leader and our General-Secretary 
of our All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, Dr . Puratchi Thalaivi Amma. Lakhs 
and lakhs of our cadre that forge to form a society. Naturally very few people can get selected 
at the hands of our Amma to get elected as Members of this august House. I have got such a 
rare opportunity as part of that society that has s haped me up to be so. I have been born 
elsewhere and each one of our from different places . Now I find myself here getting an 
opportunity to become an MP, thanks to Amma. It is also a rare opportunity to be a member 
of this House of the elders, the Rajya Sabha. The ' Vol', the tool that stands for valour and 
knowledge was provided to me by the society led by our 'Amma' and I would to record here 
that I am deeply indebted to her. I am happy to recall it here. I would like to quote another 
'new verse' on this occasion.  
'I am like an ordinary dot.  
I have been made a big shot with no blot  
by the eminent among we lot,  
puratchi thalaivi 'Amma' the great.  
Just by a stroke of her pen  
she had ensured my  
standing in this August House.  

248 Felicitation to the  [RAJYASABHA]  Retiring Members  
I consider this House a college or an University where people throng to gather knowledge. 
I have had my commissions and omissions as a studen t. As the head of a college or an 
educational institution, the Chair was kind of us e ven when we had gone beyond the brief 
and resorted to even certain mischief. You have only been affectionately chiding us like the 
Headmaster of a school. I would like to thank you for treating us kindly like your wards.  
It is green in my memory what all I have come acros s in this August House and the 
knowledge and experience I have gathered through th e interactions I have had with my 
fellow Members of Parliament. 
I can not forget for ever the rich experience I have gained.  
I have worked with three Chairmen in this House. Late Shri Krishan Kant, Shri Bhairon 
Singh Shekhawat were there. Now we have you (Shri Mohammed Ansari) here sir. I would 
like to recall my working with the then Deputy Chairman Smt. Najma Heptullah. Now, we 
have Hon'ble Rehman Khan. All of you have treated us with great affection. I would like to 
bestow my thanks again and again.  
At this juncture I would like to placeforth an appeal that is apolitical. It is a great opportunity 
to become a ruling party. Whoever or whichever party comes to power, they must discharge 
their functions with a vision and a long term perspective without any considerations having 
the next elections in the mind. We must think of the next generation and the future ahead.  
A college student an Islam by faith had written in Tamil Nadu, 'we are yet to see the 
Dawn, as we won freedom at night'. It only shows how pained he was to have said so after 
seeing all the dark in the system. Its sound echoed in this august House too. Let's have a real 
dawn. Let our lives brighten with all its brightness in our country India.  
Providing a better life to all the citizens of this country from all walks of life must be the 
vision of all those who are here in this House cutt ing across party lines. This is our duty. 
Reiterating again my grateful acknowledgements to our leader and thanking the Chair and 
fellow members again, let me conclude. I would also like to thank all the officials and security 
staff. Pointing out again that this is only an intermission let me, Perumal, this Perumal, your 
fellow member Perumal, take leave of you for now. T hank you.  
SHRI DWIJENDRANATH SHARMAH (Assam): Mr. Chairman, Sir, and hon. Members, 
six years back I came to this House with the blessings of my Leader Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, 
who brought me to this House and my first speech in this House was on the North-Eastern 
Council (Amendment) Bill. I remember very well, when I joined this House, that Bill came 
and I started speaking in the Rajya Sabha with that Bill.  
Sir, during the last six years, I believe, I tried my best to highlight the problems, particularly, 
of my State—Assam and the North-Eastern Region. It is because of the fact that my State is 
passing through a very crucial stage since long. Du ring this period, whenever there is a 
problem, we used to go to our hon. Prime Minister, whom we treat with respect, not only 
because he represents the country, but he has been representing my State—Assam — all the 
time. We take his advice whenever there is a problem. He was prompt enough to solve those 
problems which my State and my people are facing. I have already mentioned that Assam is 
passing through a crucial period for a long-time. T here are many other problems in the 
North-Eastern Region. I remember, whenever there is  a problem, I used to go to the hon. 
Home Minister. He was prompt in giving me time and trying to solve the problems pertaining
